_comment: agent 站档案的 pitfalls（头号误解）英文 —— 第 1 批（agents 与 harness 分区）。2026-10-08 A6.1 扩至含全部 26 个 agents/harness 条目。
_critical: ⚠⚠ 这是全站**最敏感**的一段内容：每一条都在纠正读者对产品的**错误理解**，很多直接关系到会不会误用（比如「以为默认是安全的 —— 默认是 full toolset 且没有沙箱层」）。
_rules: 0) **判断强度必须完全保留**。「以为 X」型误解 → 'Thinking X'；「忽略 Y」→ 'Ignoring Y'。
1) **否定强调不能丢**：原文用「**不是**」「**核验发现**」强调的地方，英文也要 bold。
2) **未核验标记保留**：「本次未核验」「核验 2026-09-30」→ not verified / checked on 2026-09-30。这是本站的诚实边界。
4) 官方引用原样（production-grade、Move from experiment to production without changing frameworks）。
aider-cli: Assuming it is still actively maintained — the latest release stopped at 2025-08-09, 13 months before collection
Assuming the models the README recommends are current — the list is still on the previous generation
Assuming auto-commit is a side effect — it is the core design, and you need to know git's undo workflow first
aider: Assuming it is an editor plugin — it is a resident Aider process plus a browser UI
Treating watch mode as a cloud background job — it needs a local process running the whole time
Not realising auto-commit applies in watch mode too, which makes it riskier under a resident process
claude-code-cli: Assuming a GitHub repo means open source — LICENSE.md is All rights reserved plus commercial terms
Overlooking the default that reads outside the working directory ask first — your first run may be interrupted
Assuming compression fixes every over-long case; the official docs still address the "still too long after compression" edge
claude-code: Assuming the IDE form is a separate product — it is one process with three entry points, same as the CLI
Carrying the CLI's permission design over to the IDE form; this round did not verify that they match
Assuming open source means free to use — the licence is proprietary
cline: Assuming it is a single-form VS Code extension — it actually has CLI, Desktop and extension
Overlooking headless mode — the CLI form supports CI/CD integration in its own right
Assuming approval behaves identically across forms: the extension explicitly has human-in-the-loop, but behaviour under CLI headless was not verified
Assuming auto-commit is by design — by default every edit needs approval, and auto-approve enables unattended runs
codex-cli: Treating API credits as part of the subscription — they are billed separately
Assuming the CLI is the whole thing — there is also an app server for custom clients
Assuming the docs site can be curled directly — a CDN may block it
codex-ide: Treating it as a standalone IDE — it is really an extension installed into an existing editor
Assuming the IDE extension and the CLI are two separate systems — the app server architecture lets them share sessions
Assuming the IDE extension has its own permission model — both share config.toml, and the sandbox and approvals are the same
copilot: Reading Flex allotment as a fixed quota — the official docs say it changes
Overlooking third-party agent delegation in Preview (Claude / Codex)
Assuming individual plans share a quota pool — pooled usage is Business / Enterprise only
Assuming the cloud agent honours content exclusion — the official docs say plainly that it does not
crush: Assuming the licence clearly permits commercial use — GitHub reports NOASSERTION and the terms were not verified
Assuming it only works with your own models — it can also connect to Anthropic / OpenAI and others
Assuming each terminal window is configured independently — within the same workspace, first-wins locks the settings
cursor: Treating Cursor as a purely local editor — since 2026-09-02 there is a self-hosted form where code need not leave your infrastructure
Treating the cloud capability as "having an entry point is enough" — the official docs are explicit that closing the laptop does not stop it
Confusing Security Review with Bugbot — one covers exploitable defects, the other style and quality issues
gemini-cli: Assuming open source means unlimited use — the free tier has clear daily limits (6,000 code requests + 240 chats/day)
Assuming the npx form pollutes your local environment — it runs temporarily with no install
Overlooking MCP support — the repository README lists it explicitly as an extensibility feature
grok-bot: Treating "separate usage" as free — the official pages only say it is billed apart from the main plan
Expecting to look up approval granularity and credential handling — the release page does not state them and this entry does not fill them in
Inferring from Grok 4.6's "focus on long-running agents" that this is what it runs — neither page names the other
Assuming it only works with SuperGrok — the official pages have already extended it to all Cursor tiers
Assuming it can pay directly the way Muse can — the official Grok Bot page never mentions payment or checkout
meta-muse: Treating Confidential VM as a shipping feature — the official docs say Later this year; it is not live
Treating Sentinel as "Muse asking first" — it is a separately isolated system agent
Assuming deleting a message erases the memory — the official docs say it may still recall what it learned
Reading "free for most" as free for everything — the boundary is not quantified and subscription pricing was not verified
Describing Muse's background permission as "the docs say read-only" — what they give is a mechanism (writes must be approved), not a read-only statement
Assuming disconnecting a Connector clears the related memory — the docs say it might still remain
Assuming forget skill guarantees erasure — the wording is "to the best of its ability"
openai-dot: Reading "proactive research" as background access to change your things — the official docs limit it to read-only tools
Assuming custom rules can relax the official limits — the docs state built-in safety requirements always apply
Treating Dot as a standalone product to subscribe to — it comes with Pro / Business Premium
Assuming it is on by default in Enterprise — the docs say it is off by default and a workspace admin must enable it
Generalising "content is not used for training" to every tier — the docs name Business / Enterprise / Edu only
Assuming background work runs to completion — the docs state safety monitoring can pause it mid-run
opencode: Reading the provider support list as entitlement — a connector being available is not the same as having a model subscription
Assuming it executes commands with full rights by default — the README says it asks before bash commands
Assuming access to a provider means it is free — model costs are still yours
windsurf: Not knowing the product is now Devin Desktop — searching for Windsurf may not find the matching docs
Assuming Teams is a single per-seat price — it is two layers: plan fee plus $40 per full-time seat
Assuming add-on usage is discounted — the official docs say it is billed at API pricing
zed: Treating Zed as yet another AI coding tool — it is an orchestration layer for three agent paths, and can use Claude / Codex / OpenCode / Cursor
Assuming the model is locked in — there are five integration paths, including local models and reusing an existing subscription
Choosing External Agent and assuming Zed governs permissions — they are determined by that agent's own auth/config
claude-agent-sdk: Assuming it is "Anthropic's version of the OpenAI Agents SDK" — **it is not**. It is the SDK for the Claude Code CLI; its capabilities come from that CLI, not from the framework
Assuming `allowed_tools` restricts the toolset — the official docs state "It does not remove tools from Claude's toolset"; use `disallowed_tools` to disable
Assuming the default is safe — the default is the **full toolset (Read/Write/Edit/Bash)**, with no sandbox layer
Assuming a system prompt change takes effect immediately — a snapshot freezes it. It lands only after a compact or a new session (unless snapshot=False)
Assuming MIT means no additional terms — Anthropic's commercial terms still apply (see the body above)

Assuming the TypeScript build is licensed like the Python one: **verification found no LICENSE file in the TS build, and the licence API returns null**. Its licensing status is unknown (checked 2026-09-30)
codex-sdk: Assuming openai/codex-sdk from the v3 roadmap exists — that repo 404s; the SDK is a subdirectory of the monorepo
Assuming the SDK version number reflects the capability — package.json says 0.0.0-dev; the real version tracks the CLI (currently 0.159.3)
Expecting it to work out of the box outside a Git directory — the CLI requires the working directory to be a Git repository, so you must skip explicitly
Treating `sandbox_workspace_write.network_access` and the SDK's `networkAccessEnabled` as two separate things — the latter is the SDK-level entry point; the former is a config passthrough
Treating OpenAI Agents SDK (a pure Python library) as a like-for-like alternative — the forms differ, see layer_position
crewai: Assuming it is a role-play toy — the official positioning is production-grade, and the README states "Move from experiment to production without changing frameworks"
Taking Crew Control Plane's capabilities as built into the open version — tracing, centralised control, enterprise security, 24×7 support and local/cloud deployment are CrewAI AMP selling points
Treating guardrails as a permission boundary — the official docs state they validate task output only, never input, and there is no sandbox
Assuming memory and knowledge are two separate memory systems — knowledge is a RAG fact store, memory is the unified record store
Assuming checkpointing is a later concern — the official docs already ship Json and Sqlite backends plus a resume CLI, so it can be enabled on demand
Assuming a Flow gives you vendor-hosted background execution — Flow provides state management; the process still runs on your own machine
deepagents: Treating Deep Agents / LangChain / LangGraph as one thing — the official docs are explicit that these are three layers with different responsibilities (see `layer_position`)
Reading "trust the LLM" as a product feature rather than a risk warning — the official text tells you to set boundaries at the tool/sandbox layer yourself
Assuming open source means zero cost — model inference plus LangSmith (the officially recommended tracing/eval) both cost money
Assuming the latest version is 0.7.0 — a competitor site snapshotted 0.7.0; **it is actually 0.7.20** (checked 2026-09-30)
google-adk: Assuming it is "Google's version of the OpenAI Agents SDK" — **it is an orchestration framework** whose core asset is the Workflow Runtime graph engine, not single-agent primitives
Reading `state management` as "has context management" — the former is process state; the latter is the separate Context Compaction mechanism (1.16+)
Treating MCP as a core dependency — the README lists MCP only as one tool source, which is not the same as OpenAI Agents SDK putting `mcp>=1.19.0` in `dependencies`
Assuming Tool Confirmation equals a sandbox — it is "ask once before running", not a boundary
Assuming open source and free means zero cost — Cloud Run / Vertex Agent Engine costs are yours, and there is a `GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_ENTERPRISE` switch
Assuming it is Python-only — there is a separate TypeScript repo (`google/adk-js`, 1,426★); the Python body is the only thing indexed here
Mixing up repo names — the sample repo shows as `google/adk-recipes` while the description says adk-samples
hermes-agent: Using it as a programming framework — **it is a general personal assistant**; coding is one of many things it does, and its form is nothing like LangGraph/CrewAI
Taking "the only agent with a built-in learning loop" as this site's conclusion — **that is the vendor's marketing line; this site ran no cross-product comparison**
Reading the seven terminal backends as seven deployment modes — the official text says terminal backends (the backend that executes tools), and Modal/Daytona there provide **sleep**, not always-on
Assuming `/compress` is automatic — **it is an explicit command**; nothing is compressed unless you trigger it
Overlooking DM pairing — for an agent that reaches six messaging platforms and touches your filesystem, who can command it is the central safety question
Running `hermes claw migrate` without reading the dry-run first — the command touches API keys (the README lists five providers)
Migrating without confirming — this site's view of the Hermes / OpenClaw relationship was not verified; it records only the README's first-hand facts
langgraph: Treating Deep Agents and LangGraph as two competitors — **Deep Agents is a higher-level package built on LangGraph** (the README says so)

Using releases/latest to judge the version — **latest on a monorepo is unreliable**: on this entry latest returned `cli==0.4.32.dev0` (a sub-package dev build); the main package version has to be picked out of the release list (1.2.12 at the time of this check)
Reading checkpoint persistence as "context management" — a checkpoint stores **graph state**; context compression and memory are a separate layer the README calls memory
Assuming it ships a filesystem or a tool system — it handles neither; wire up your own, or go through Deep Agents
Assuming interrupts are a permission guardrail — they "check and modify state"; they do not draw file or network boundaries
Assuming that installing LangGraph is enough — the official front page points you at LangSmith for debugging and deployment, and that is a commercial product
llamaindex: Reading 52k★ as "an actively developed orchestration framework" — **the official front page states the primary focus has shifted to document parsing**
Assuming workflow / agent orchestration lives in the OSS — the README puts Workflows in the section about the commercial LlamaAgents platform
Conflating LlamaIndex's "data connectors" with Deep Agents' "filesystem" — the former is data-source ingestion and parsing, the latter is an agent's workspace file operations
Treating LlamaParse as a free open-source component — it is a commercial platform and you must sign up for a key
Reading 300+ integrations as equally reliable — the official wording is "work seamlessly"; this site has not measured how well they align
Missing the NOTE the README writes about itself — "This README is not updated as frequently as the documentation"
openai-agents-sdk: Reading "provider-agnostic" as "switching providers costs nothing" — the docs promise 100+ without a quantified guarantee; this site marks it unverified
Assuming SandboxAgent works out of the box on Windows — the local path is only `UnixLocalSandboxClient` (macOS/Linux); Windows needs Docker or hosted
Assuming Guardrails work as a permission boundary — they are input/output validation, not a sandbox boundary; they address different risk types

Assuming this is an official shell around OpenAI's closed-source SDK — it is itself an MIT-licensed framework, and the official docs state they are "committed to continuing to build the Agents SDK as an open source framework"
openhands: Assuming it is a Python SDK — **the main repo is a TypeScript web control centre**; the programming entry point is `OpenHands/software-agent-sdk` (a further 1,190★)
Judging by the repo name and description that it is an "AI-driven software development tool" — **the README's front-page title is now Agent Canvas**, and the positioning is a control centre
Assuming it competes with Codex SDK / Claude Agent SDK — **it is their orchestration layer** (the README says it can run those agents)
Going straight to Option 1 in production — the official docs put a WARNING on that option: the agent has full access to your filesystem
Reading `--public` mode as "more convenient" — it is the safeguard that keeps the key out of the front end, meant for non-local access
Assuming "has run history" means "has context management" — the former is state; the latter has its own mechanism (LLMSummarizingCondenser / RollingCondenser)

Assuming it uses ACP only and does not support MCP — the MCP Servers page says both the CLI and the Canvas can configure it (http / sse / stdio plus Bearer / API Key / OAuth); ACP is the separate line for orchestrating third-party agents
context7: Assuming it is a purely local tool — queries actually go to Upstash's remote servers
Omitting a version number gets you mismatched docs — the README calls out "Specify a Version" specifically
Assuming open source means fully local — the code is MIT but the core is a hosted service
everything: Assuming it is a usable all-in-one tool server — the official docs say it is a test server
Enabling it in production — it was never positioned as production-ready
Assuming more tools means more usefulness — these tools demonstrate protocol features rather than serve real purposes
fetch: Enabling it directly where the intranet is reachable — the official docs warn it can reach local and internal IPs
Assuming it fetches pages behind a login — it is a stateless fetch
Assuming the output is clean Markdown — the structure varies with the target page
filesystem: Assuming the official repo's server is production-ready — the README states it is a reference implementation only
Starting it without a directory argument — it errors at initialisation rather than silently touching the whole disk
Assuming that withholding write tools prevents file changes — write_file / edit_file do write
git: Assuming it is read-only — it can commit and switch branches
ag2: Assuming `pip install ag2` is still classic AutoGen — since v1.0 ConversableAgent / GroupChat / `import autogen` all moved to the ag2-classic package
Assuming ag2 is a smooth upgrade from autogen — officially v1.0 is not a drop-in upgrade; the agent model, orchestration, and imports all changed
Assuming it is a Microsoft-official project — it is maintained by community volunteers (ag2ai), a different line from Microsoft's Microsoft Agent Framework
Assuming `blocked=[...]` is a security boundary — officially it is only best-effort; isolation in the restricted shell comes from the `allowed` allowlist and `readonly`
amp: Assuming tools run only after approval — officially, Amp does not ask for approval before running tools.
Expecting a standalone VS Code extension — integration is via the CLI and `ide connect` (VS Code / Cursor / Windsurf / Zed / Neovim).
Treating $20/mo as the whole cost — orbs are billed by the minute and overage is charged against credits.
continue: Assuming Continue is still actively maintained — the repo README now states it is "no longer actively maintained and is read-only for all users".
Assuming the old Hub commercial price list still applies — the site is now an acquisition notice and continue.dev/pricing returns 404.
Assuming models come with included quota — the extension itself is free and open source, but model costs are yours (bring your own provider or run local Ollama).
copilot-cli: Thinking Copilot CLI is a separate purchase — it comes with a Copilot subscription and has no standalone price
Thinking the CLI costs no quota — each prompt deducts one premium request, and premium models multiply it
Taking the about page's plan list (Pro/Pro+/Business/Enterprise) as the only wording — the quickstart page says all plans
cursor-cli: Thinking Cursor CLI is a standalone free tool: it needs a Cursor account or an API key, and usage draws on the same account quota pools.
Assuming print mode writes files by default: the headless page states that without --force / --yolo changes are only proposed, not applied.
Expecting Shell Mode to run long tasks: commands time out after 30 seconds and the limit is not configurable.
factory-droid: Assuming BYOK has no quota — official docs state Individual plans include only an allowance of free BYOK usage
Treating Droid as CLI-only, when the vendor actually leads with CLI + desktop App + SDK
Expecting droid exec to edit files, when it defaults to read-only mode
goose: Assuming approval is on by default — it runs in Autonomous mode and will execute commands and edit files without asking.
Assuming it only writes code — the official positioning is a general-purpose agent (research, writing, automation, data analysis).
Assuming it works right after install — you must configure an LLM provider first (`goose configure`).
jules: Treating the old beta docs' "2 concurrent / 5 total tasks per day" as today's free tier
Assuming API-created sessions wait for you to approve the plan — they auto-approve by default
Mistaking Jules for a local/IDE live agent — it is an asynchronous cloud agent
junie: Assuming Junie is a standalone IDE — it is a plugin inside JetBrains IDEs (plus a separate CLI form)
Assuming Junie is available under the AI Enterprise tier — the official page states that tier does not currently include Junie
Assuming MCP remote servers work — the docs state only the stdio transport is currently supported
kiro: Treating Kiro as an IDE-only tool: there is also CLI / Web / Mobile and Crew, and a Cloud Session keeps running after shutdown
Assuming credits are model-specific — Kiro uses one credit pool and each model consumes it by a multiplier (up to 4.4x)
Taking Kiro Free as a long-term free tier — it is 50 credits/month, limited to open-weight models and specific Claude models
mastra: Assuming Mastra is entirely Apache-2.0 and free - the `ee/` directory is source-available and needs an enterprise licence for production; the repo licence API returns NOASSERTION
Treating Mastra Studio / observability / hosted deployment as part of the framework - those are Mastra platform products, billed on Starter $0 / Teams $250 / Enterprise tiers
Taking the README's "40+ providers" as the ceiling - the official `/models` directory page states 213 providers / 7815 models
Assuming local models need code changes - the official path is an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with LMStudio recommended, configured via `id` + `url`
microsoft-agent-framework: Treating it as "yet another new framework" — officially it is the successor of Semantic Kernel + AutoGen, built by the same teams
Assuming it is .NET-only — officially it is Python and C#/.NET with consistent APIs, plus a separate Go repo (microsoft/agent-framework-go)
Assuming it is already GA — the official overview marks it public preview and the Python install requires --pre
Assuming AutoGen / AG2 code upgrades as-is — official migration guides exist, and both the agent model and the APIs changed; it is not a drop-in
Reading a workflow checkpoint as context compression — checkpoints persist superstep-level workflow state, a different mechanism from conversational memory
pydantic-ai: Assuming it is a purely thin harness — the official Pydantic AI Harness now bundles memory, guardrails, sub-agents and context management as capabilities, plus a complete Coder agent.

Reading "durability" as "conversation storage" — official docs state plainly that "Durability is not storage": the durable engine only keeps a run alive, while thread persistence is a separate module.
Assuming evals / observability require Pydantic Logfire — official docs state instrumentation is standard OpenTelemetry, so any OTLP backend works.
Assuming A2A is a long-term built-in — the official docs mark `Agent.to_a2a()` as deprecated in 1.x and removed in 2.0, with `fasta2a` moved to datalayer/fasta2a.
smolagents: Treating `LocalPythonExecutor` as a security sandbox — the official docs state it is not a security boundary and can be bypassed.
Assuming it is only for writing code — the official positioning is a barebones library for *agents*; `CodeAgent` just expresses actions as code.
Assuming it ships hosted execution or resumable runs — it is a pure library: stop the process and it stops, and memory is not persisted to disk.
warp: Assuming Free means unlimited agent use — the official page says "Limited cloud agents access"
Assuming auto-approve bypasses the command denylist — a team denylist set in the Admin Panel is never bypassed
Assuming open source means entirely free — the client is open source, but cloud agents and Warp Drive are metered by tier
